In Chapter 21 the quest reaches Olympus, where gods who have been distant figures speak face to face with a twelve-year-old.","enduringUnderstanding":"A narrator's voice shapes how readers judge other characters, and a character's words and actions reveal power, responsibility, and loyalty.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 33, students read Chapter 22 (pp. 354–369) and see how the plot twist and rising tension follow from this confrontation.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students will analyze dialogue to explain relationships and power dynamics. How was the story different?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why can the same event sound different depending on who tells it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The person telling it picks what to say. If they're mad at someone, they make that person sound worse. If they're the hero in their own story, they leave out the parts that make them look bad."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today Percy tells us about a meeting with two of the most powerful gods. For each word, write the root, prefix, and suffix if it has them, then write the meaning in your own words."},{"type":"teach","text":""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's model with *conscious* (p. 344). The root is *sci*, from Latin, meaning 'to know.' The prefix *con-* means 'with' or 'together,' and the ending *-ous* means 'full of.' So conscious means 'full of knowing,' or aware. Percy uses it when he is waking up and becoming aware of where he is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Now try *restrained* (p. 345). Find the prefix, root, and suffix. What might it mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The prefix is *re-*, the root is *strain* (to pull tight), and the suffix is *-ed*. It means pulled back or held back, like when someone holds in their anger."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *instinctively* (p. 350) and *interjected* (p. 349). What parts help you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"*Instinctively* has *instinct* plus *-ive* and *-ly*, so it means in a way that comes from instinct. *Interjected* has the prefix *inter-*, meaning between, and the root *ject*, meaning throw. So someone throws words in between other people's talking."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Quickly cover the rest. *Gratitude*: root *grat* (thankful) plus *-itude* (state of). *Condemned*: prefix *con-* plus root *demn* (to judge as guilty) plus *-ed*. *Deserve*: prefix *de-* plus root *serv* (serve, earn). *Pleaded*: base *plead* plus *-ed*. *Falsetto*: Italian for 'a little false' voice; the root *fals* means untrue. *Twinge*: no useful affixes; learn it from context as a quick sharp feeling."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Students put each word in the organizer and revisit them during reading. Words with no clear affixes, like twinge, should be marked 'context clues.' Many roots connect to Spanish: conciencia, gratitud, condenado, merecer."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners use word parts and context to build precise meaning for the ten words.","sayAsk":"Say each word aloud with a partner and clap the syllables. Ask: Which word part do you already know? Use the frames: The word ___ has the root ___, which means ___. I think ___ means ___ because ___. Point out cognates such as gratitude/gratitud and condemned/condenado.","watchFor":"If students guess only from sound, then prompt: What does the root tell you? If students can name each part but not the meaning, then have them act out or draw the word. Success: students explain the meaning using at least one word part."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: dividing words into parts","tryThis":"Give a bank of common prefixes (con-, re-, de-, inter-) and suffixes (-ed, -ly, -ous) so students match instead of invent. Make a three-column chart for Percy, Zeus, and Poseidon. In each column, record at least two pieces of dialogue or action. Next to each, write one word showing power, anger, forgiveness, or distance. Use vocabulary words where they fit."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Look at what characters say and do. A line of dialogue shows what a character wants to say. An action, such as Poseidon being restrained or Zeus pointing a finger, shows what they feel under the words. Together they show relationships."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Zeus treat Percy and Poseidon in this scene? What evidence shows it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Zeus acts like he has all the power. He is angry and suspicious, and he talks to Poseidon like Poseidon is guilty. His words are sharp and he threatens Percy, which shows he doesn't trust his brother."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do Poseidon's words and actions show about how he feels about Percy and about Zeus?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Poseidon protects Percy and speaks more calmly than Zeus. He is still stiff and distant with his brother, so he seems to care about his son but is not ready to make up with Zeus."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy respond when the gods argue? What does that show about him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy is nervous but speaks up and says what he knows. He is brave because he talks to powerful gods and does not hide, even though he is a kid."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Page-level details vary by edition. Circulate and have students point to specific lines. Accept any word choice they can support with a quote."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.3"],"stem":"In pp. 344–353, how do the characters' responses show the relationship between Zeus and Poseidon?","choices":[{"text":"They fully trust each other and agree right away.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may assume that a resolution means closeness. The brothers' words and actions still show suspicion and distance."},{"text":"Zeus shows anger and power while Poseidon stays more controlled, and the two remain somewhat distant.","correct":true,"rationale":"This matches the contrast in how they speak and act toward each other throughout the scene."},{"text":"Poseidon is the angriest and tries to take Zeus's bolt.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reflects the earlier suspicion that Poseidon is the thief; the confrontation clears him of it."},{"text":"Neither god pays attention to Percy.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may overlook that the gods speak to Percy and his actions drive the resolution."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining characters' feelings and relationships with evidence.","sayAsk":"Say: Zeus ___ (verb) because ___. Encourage present tense for literary analysis (Zeus shouts, Percy speaks).","watchFor":"If students retell without evidence, then prompt: Which line shows that? If students switch between past and present tense, then model: The text shows... Success: students pair a quote with a verb of feeling or power."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing evidence","tryThis":"Give a short list of page spots to reread and ask 'What does he say? What does he do?' for each. A theme is a bigger idea the story shows through details. Let's practice both for this scene. When you write, use correct grammar: complete sentences, a subject and verb that agree, and present tense for analysis."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think alone for one minute, then pair, then share. Answer: How does the confrontation resolve the conflict over the missing master bolt and helm? Then choose a theme (power, responsibility, or family loyalty) and cite one detail that expresses it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this scene settle the conflict over the master bolt and the helm?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy returns the bolt to Zeus and the helm is also dealt with, so Zeus learns Poseidon did not steal it. The threat of war between the gods ends."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which theme do you see, and what detail shows it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"One theme is family loyalty. Poseidon defends Percy even though the gods are not close, which shows that family ties matter even when people are in conflict."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How is a summary different from your opinion of the scene?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A summary says what happened: Percy returns the bolt and the gods stop fighting. An opinion would say whether I think Zeus was fair, which I would write separately."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Listen for the difference between summary and judgment. If a student says 'Zeus is a jerk,' redirect: What does Zeus say or do that shows this?"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students summarize and state a theme with present-tense verbs and academic language.","sayAsk":"Say: First retell with a partner, then say the theme. Frames: The conflict is resolved when ___. One theme is ___. This detail shows ___. Verbs: shows, reveals, resolves, protects.","watchFor":"If students give opinion language ('I think Zeus was mean'), then prompt: Rewrite it as what the text shows. If students name a theme in one word, then ask for a full sentence. Success: a complete sentence with a theme and a detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: summary versus opinion","tryThis":"Have students underline facts (who did what) in their summary and cross out any 'I think' or 'unfair' words."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Ready for extension: Ask students to connect two themes (such as power and responsibility) in one sentence and explain how the resolution shows both."}]}]},{"id":"lia-narration-pov","title":"Part C: Percy's Voice","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.6","RL.6.4","L.6.1","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 21","pages":"pp. 344–353"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Percy tells the story in first person, so we only see what he notices and how he interprets it. His modern, casual attitude also makes the gods feel less distant and sometimes less scary, and more like people."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread a short passage where Percy describes Zeus or Poseidon. Annotate what he notices, how he interprets expressions and words, and which details he emphasizes. Then write 4–5 sentences: How does Percy's narration shape how we see Zeus and Poseidon? How might the scene feel different if it were told in the past tense by a distant narrator? Use at least one vocabulary word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy notice about Zeus and Poseidon that helps us form an opinion of them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy notices their expressions, their voices, and how they treat each other. Because he describes Zeus as angry and Poseidon as calmer, we see Zeus as harsh and Poseidon as kinder."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy's modern attitude affect how we see the gods?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"His casual, honest voice makes the gods seem less like far-off legends and more like a frustrated family. We care about their feelings, not just their power."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If this scene were told by a distant narrator in the past, how might it feel different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A distant narrator might make Zeus and Poseidon sound grand and formal, like myths. We might not know Percy's fears and reactions, so the scene would feel less personal."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence frames: Percy notices ___, which makes readers see Zeus as ___. By describing ___, the narrator shows ___. If the story were told by ___, the scene would feel ___."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Check grammar while students write: complete sentences, subject-verb agreement, and consistent present tense in analysis (L.6.1)."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in evaluating how the narrator's language choices shape perception.","sayAsk":"Say: Percy's words make readers see ___. Ask: Which word or detail shows his attitude? Frames: Percy describes ___ as ___. This choice makes Zeus seem ___. A different narrator would ___.","watchFor":"If students say 'Percy is funny' but not why it matters, then prompt: How does that change how we see the gods? If tenses are mixed, then model present tense. Success: students connect a narrator's word choice to the reader's view."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting narration to perception","tryThis":"Give two sentences describing Zeus, one in Percy's voice and one formal. Ask which one makes him seem scarier or friendlier, and why."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Ready for extension: Ask students to rewrite two sentences from the scene in third person past tense with a distant narrator and explain what is gained and lost."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students consolidate their thinking about the confrontation and the narrator's influence, and link it to the performance task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-exit-ticket","title":"Exit Ticket","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.6","RL.6.2"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Connect to the Performance Task: In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students will analyze dialogue to explain relationships and power dynamics. This shows the theme of ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 21, Percy's narration makes readers see Zeus as angry and controlling and Poseidon as protective because he describes their tone and how they treat Percy.
